guides.title: What the engine does
guides.lede: One container turns text into a finished document: paginated, branded, illustrated, censored where it must be, and checked before it leaves.
guides.meta_description: One container turns text into a finished document: paginated, branded, illustrated, censored where it must be, and checked before it leaves.

blocks.html: Three input formats, one rendering pipeline, one contract. Whatever you send — Markdown, raw HTML or a Tera template with its data — the document goes through the same expansion, the same stylesheet assembly and the same engine, so a feature documented here works on all three.

head: Stage
What happens
Guide
rows: CENSOR tags and regions are removed from the source, before anything else sees it.
→ Censoring: hiding what must not ship
options.cover prepends a cover page, styled by the theme.
default.css, then the theme, then your css, then the layout options.
pandoc and/or WeasyPrint produce the PDF. Identical inputs hit the cache.
options.autolayout inspects the result and re-renders it if that improves it.

cards.title: Markdown → PDF
cards.html: POST /api/convert. pandoc, tables, footnotes, table of contents, code highlighting.

cards.title: HTML → PDF
cards.html: POST /api/html-to-pdf. For markup you already build client-side.

cards.title: Template → PDF
cards.html: POST /api/render. A Tera (Jinja2-like) template plus a JSON context — the invoice case.

cards.title: → PNG pages
cards.html: POST /api/preview. One page, a range, or a contact sheet.

cards.title: → Redacted, compared
cards.html: redact paints out and flattens; diff compares two renders pixel by pixel.

blocks.html: Every endpoint that produces a PDF returns the binary PDF — unless you send both client_id and pdf_name, in which case the file is saved and you get a JSON download URL instead. Nothing else changes.

The three optional fields appear only when they apply — cached when the PDF came from the render cache, warnings when a chart or diagram could not be drawn, layout when you asked for autolayout. A client written before they existed still parses the response.

guides.title: First call in three minutes
guides.lede: No SDK, no build step: HTTP, JSON, and a key in a header.
guides.meta_description: No SDK, no build step: HTTP, JSON, and a key in a header.

blocks.html: Every /api/* route needs your key, as X-API-Key or Authorization: Bearer. Two routes stay open: GET /api/health (the container probe) and GET /download/… (fetching a PDF that was already produced). The public tools at AI SmartTalk Documents need no key at all.

blocks.code:
# Your key comes from your personal space — never hard-coded in a repository
export MDTOPDF_KEY='your-key'

curl -s $BASE/api/health
# {"status":"ok","version":"0.2.0","engines":["weasyprint","wkhtmltopdf","pdflatex"]}

curl -X POST "$BASE/api/convert" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"markdown": "# Hello\n\nA **document**.", "options": {"page_numbers": true}}' \
  --output document.pdf

blocks.text: Or keep it on the server

blocks.html: Add client_id and pdf_name and the answer becomes a URL. This is what you want whenever the PDF will be chained into merge, watermark, protect, redact or diff — those endpoints take download paths, not uploads.
client_id and pdf_name are plain names — [A-Za-z0-9._-], 128 characters at most, not starting with a dot. They build a path on disk, so anything else is refused with a 400.
Every field of options is optional, and an options object that does not mention a field renders exactly as it did before that field existed. Nothing here is breaking.

head: Field
Values
Effect
rows: Table of contents built from the headings.
Diagonal CSS watermark, drawn at render time.
Cover page, styled by the theme.
Wording of censored blocks with no named level.
Audits the output and corrects it. Costs a full extra render.

blocks.html: Errors are always JSON: {"error": "…", "details": "…"}. Every response carries an X-Request-Id; send your own on the way in and it is echoed back and attached to every log event — that is what ties a support ticket to what the service actually did.

guides.title: Themes and cover pages
guides.lede: Three brand kits ship with the service. They are named, versioned and immutable — a contract rendered with report@1 still comes out identical next year.
guides.meta_description: Three brand kits ship with the service. They are named, versioned and immutable — a contract rendered with report@1 still comes out identical next year.

blocks.html: A theme is a whole stylesheet, not a colour: typography, headings, tables, callouts, footnotes, table of contents and — when the kit ships one — a cover page. Ask for it with options.theme, as "name" for the latest version or "name@2" to pin one.
Pulled live from GET /api/themes on the service you are pointing at, previews included. What you see below is what this deployment will actually render.
Every kit understands the same two pandoc div conventions, so a document can move from one theme to another without being rewritten.

blocks.code:
::: success
**Target met.** Median render time is back under two seconds.
:::

::: warning
The figures for December are still provisional.
:::

::: wide
| A wide table | rendered | at a reduced | body size |
|--------------|----------|--------------|-----------|
| …            | …        | …            | …         |
:::

head: Class
Use
rows: A table with many columns — rendered at a reduced body size so it still fits.
Callout boxes, coloured by the theme's tokens.

blocks.html: options.cover inserts a cover page in front of the document. When the theme ships a cover.html it is used and styled by the kit; otherwise a built-in, self-contained template takes over so a cover asked for without a theme is still a cover page. Every value is escaped, and a logo URL goes through the same fetch policy as any other asset in the document.
Preview a kit's cover without rendering anything of your own: GET /api/themes/report/latest/preview.png?cover=true.
A theme is a directory on the server, read once at startup. A kit that does not validate is dropped with a warning rather than keeping the service from starting.

blocks.code:
themes/
└── acme/
    └── v1/                 # exactly v1, v2, … — v01 is refused
        ├── theme.json      # required: label, description, fonts, colors
        ├── theme.css       # required, non-empty, 512 KB max
        ├── cover.html      # optional — Tera: title, subtitle, logo, date
        ├── header.html     # optional — used unless the request overrides it
        └── footer.html     # optional

blocks.html: Themes are immutable. The render cache key contains name@version, so changing a published theme.css in place does not invalidate anything — the old PDF keeps being served until the cache TTL expires. Any visual change means a new v<n+1> directory.

The fonts a kit declares all ship inside the image. Naming a family that is not installed does not fail the render — it silently falls back, which is exactly the kind of difference nobody notices until the contract is printed.

guides.title: Headers, footers and CSS
guides.lede: Four ways to reach the same stylesheet, in a defined order. Knowing that order is the difference between styling a document and fighting it.
guides.meta_description: Four ways to reach the same stylesheet, in a defined order. Knowing that order is the difference between styling a document and fighting it.

blocks.html: Stylesheets are concatenated, later wins on equal specificity:

blocks.code: templates/default.css  →  theme.css  →  your `css` field  →  `options` (paper, margins, numbering, watermark)

blocks.html: templates/default.css is the floor every document stands on: readable typography, tables, page-break rules, and the geometry of censored blocks. It is applied even when no theme is asked for, which is why an unstyled request still comes out looking deliberate.

Four fields, resolved in a strict priority: inline HTML beats a named template, and a named template beats the fragment the theme ships. That order is what lets one document override a brand kit for one page without abandoning the kit.

head: Field
Priority
Content
rows: Raw HTML, sent in the request.
The name of a file in templates/, e.g. header.html.
Used when the request names neither.

blocks.html: These sit in templates/ and are ready to be named in a request. They are examples as much as they are assets — copy one, change the logo and the wording, drop it next to them.

head: File
What it draws
rows: The neutral starting point: a logo slot (empty src) and a company name, on a ruled line. Copy this one.
A centred page number above a rule, fixed to the bottom of the page.
A filled-in example: MDP Data Protection branding.
Not a header — the base stylesheet described above.

blocks.html: For page numbering, prefer options.page_numbers over a custom footer: it uses the CSS paged-media counters the engine already sets up, and it survives a change of theme. A footer template is for what numbering cannot express — a legal mention, a document reference, a classification level.

HTML headers and footers only make sense for the HTML-based engines. With engine: "pdflatex" they are ignored and the service says so in its logs rather than silently producing a document without them.
The css field is appended last, so it wins. Everything CSS Paged Media offers is available — running headers, named pages, breaks:

guides.title: Censoring: hiding what must not ship
guides.lede: The censored text is removed from the source before pandoc ever sees it. It cannot be selected, searched or extracted from the PDF, because it is not in the PDF.
guides.meta_description: The censored text is removed from the source before pandoc ever sees it. It cannot be selected, searched or extracted from the PDF, because it is not in…

blocks.html: This is the feature the fork was built for: publishing one document to two audiences. The premium reader gets everything; everyone else gets the same document with a sized, labelled hole where the paid content was — which is a sales pitch, not an error page.

head: Tag
Effect
rows: Point replacement: the historical blurred block. Unchanged since day one.
The same, labelled with that level.
Removes the region; the block is sized after what was removed, so the page keeps its shape.
Keeps the first 25 words, removes the rest. The teaser.
Removes a run of text without breaking the paragraph around it.

blocks.html: The historical point tag tolerates spacing: {{CENSOR}}, {{ CENSOR }}, {{CENSOR }} and {{ CENSOR}} all render exactly what they always rendered. Levels are free-form names — premium, confidentiel, interne, secret are the ones in common use. Modifiers combine with a comma: {{CENSOR:start,confidentiel}}.

blocks.code:
# Market study 2026

## Public summary

The market grew by 18% over the quarter.

## Margins by segment

{{CENSOR:teaser=20,premium}}
The hardware segment carries a gross margin of 34%, well above the
services segment, whose contracts are priced on a three-year horizon and
absorb the onboarding cost in the first year.
{{CENSOR:end}}

## Method

Our estimate rests on {{CENSOR:inline}}a proprietary panel of 400 firms{{CENSOR:end}}
weighted by revenue.

blocks.html: Two documents from one source: send it as-is for the free edition, strip the tags before sending for the paid one. Same rendering path, same pagination, same theme.

Labels cascade: the level named on the tag wins, then options.censor_label, then the historical wording. A long label wraps rather than being clipped — it is the sales pitch, and half of it would sell nothing.

blocks.text: What happens when you get it wrong

blocks.html: Malformed input always errs towards censoring. A syntax mistake must not be a way to reveal what was meant to be hidden:

head: Mistake
Behaviour
rows: Censored to the end of the document.
Depth-counted, so the outer one still closes correctly.
Opens a region — that is what a misspelled start looks like.

blocks.html: Censoring hides text you control, in a source you are about to render. To black out text in a PDF that already exists — someone else's contract, a scanned invoice — you want /api/redact, which works on pixels. See the redaction guide.

guides.title: Charts, drawn in-process
guides.lede: A fenced ```chart block becomes inline SVG. No browser, no headless Chrome, no external service — and no chart can fail your request.
guides.meta_description: A fenced ```chart block becomes inline SVG. No browser, no headless Chrome, no external service — and no chart can fail your request.

head: type
For
rows: Vertical bars — the default reflex for a few categories.
Horizontal bars — when the labels are long.
Several series compared category by category.
A trend over an ordered axis.
The same, when the volume under the curve matters.
A share of a whole, up to 8 slices.

head: Field
Default
Description
rows: Drawn inside the SVG, so they travel with the figure.
Hatch patterns, so the chart survives being printed in black and white.

blocks.html: texture is on by default on purpose. A report is printed, photocopied and faxed; two series that differ only by hue become one series the moment the colour is gone.

A block that cannot be rendered — invalid JSON, an unknown type, too many series — stays in the document as a code block, and the reason comes back in the warnings field of the JSON response. A hundred-page report is never lost over one malformed figure.
options.charts: false turns off the expansion of both block types — useful when you are rendering untrusted input and want no block expansion at all.

guides.title: Mermaid diagrams
guides.lede: Flowcharts, sequences and state machines written as text, rendered to SVG inside the page.
guides.meta_description: Flowcharts, sequences and state machines written as text, rendered to SVG inside the page.

blocks.html: Attributes may follow the language — theme=dark, title="…" — including in pandoc form ({.mermaid theme=forest}). The HTML spelling <pre><code class="language-mermaid"> works too, which matters when the Markdown was produced by another tool. Accepted themes: default, dark, forest, neutral.
click directives lose their hyperlink on purpose: a diagram in a printed report should not carry a live link to somewhere the reader cannot see.

Diagrams depend on an external service. Rendering is delegated to Mermaid Studio, so the container needs outbound access to it. If it is unreachable, times out, or is explicitly disabled, every diagram degrades to its code block plus one warning and the document still comes out. Charts have no such dependency — they are drawn in-process.

One consequence worth knowing: the render cache key is computed on the expanded source, so a document containing a diagram calls Mermaid Studio before it can hit the disk cache. An in-process diagram cache keeps that cheap, but it empties on restart — the first render of a diagram after a deployment always goes over the network.

guides.title: Layout Doctor
guides.lede: The service reads back the PDF it just produced, finds what a proofreader would find, and fixes it — but only if fixing it actually helped.
guides.meta_description: The service reads back the PDF it just produced, finds what a proofreader would find, and fixes it — but only if fixing it actually helped.

blocks.html: options.autolayout: true on any rendering endpoint analyses the produced PDF, re-renders it with corrective CSS while that improves the score, and returns the report in the layout field. A corrective pass that does not improve the score is thrown away: the client never receives a PDF worse than the one it would have had.

head: kind
Severity
Meaning
rows: Content past the page edge (error) or past the margin (warn).
A page with no ink at all — reported, not fixable.
A last page carrying almost nothing.
A heading alone at the bottom of a page.
A table cut across a page break.
A table taller than a page; suppresses the anti-break rule.

blocks.text: Auditing a PDF you already have

blocks.html: POST /api/layout runs the same analysis on an existing PDF without touching it — a useful gate in a pipeline that renders elsewhere.

It costs a full extra render per corrective pass, plus the analysis itself — roughly double the latency of the same request without it. Turn it on for documents a human will read, not for a batch of ten thousand invoices.

guides.title: Redaction and visual diff
guides.lede: Black out a PDF so the text is genuinely gone, and compare two renders pixel by pixel so a rendering regression cannot ship unnoticed.
guides.meta_description: Black out a PDF so the text is genuinely gone, and compare two renders pixel by pixel so a rendering regression cannot ship unnoticed.

blocks.html: Paints out patterns and personal data, then rebuilds every page from pixels. The redacted strings are gone from the file, and so is every text layer, bookmark, annotation and metadata entry of the source. The result is neither selectable nor searchable, and it is larger — that is the trade, and it is the only honest one.
Entities are validated by their check digits, so a 14-digit invoice number is not mistaken for a SIRET and a random 16-digit reference is not blacked out as a card number.

patterns are literal strings, not regular expressions. Comparison ignores case and normalises whitespace, so a match may span a line break. A pattern that looks like a regex (\d{4}, [A-Z]+, .*, (?i)) is rejected with a 400 rather than matched literally — receiving a document where nothing was blacked out while believing the job was done is the failure this prevents.

mode is always flatten: there is deliberately no overlay mode that would keep the text layer under a black rectangle. The binary form of the endpoint (no client_id) cannot carry the redaction counts — use the JSON form whenever you need proof of what was painted.

A PDF that was scanned — no text layer — comes back flattened with redactions: []. Nothing could be located; there is no OCR. An empty array is the only signal, and it means "nothing was found", not "nothing was there".
Compares two saved PDFs page by page and tells you whether anything moved. This is the endpoint that turns "the report still looks right" into a CI check.

threshold defaults to 0: any page that visibly moved makes the verdict changed. Raise it to tolerate noise — a CI that defaulted to tolerance would report identical on a renamed heading, which is the one thing it exists to catch.

Run a diff right after a deployment that changed the renderer without bumping the internal cache version and it will compare a stale cached PDF against a fresh one — or worse, call two different renders identical. Render both sides of a comparison in the same session.

guides.title: Upload a file, then chain tools
guides.lede: One upload, one opaque handle, and every tool in the service accepts it — including on documents this engine never rendered.
guides.meta_description: One upload, one opaque handle, and every tool in the service accepts it — including on documents this engine never rendered.

blocks.html: For a long time every tool here only worked on documents the service had produced itself, because the only way to name a file was /download/<client_id>/<name>.pdf. POST /api/files is the other half: you hand over bytes, you get a handle, and that handle goes wherever a download path went.
This is the only endpoint of the API that is not JSON: multipart/form-data, with a field named file that may repeat. Do not set Content-Type by hand — the multipart boundary is part of it.

The kind is read from the bytes, never from the extension: a .pdf that is really a zip comes back as what it is, and the tool that would have choked on it refuses before starting. What is kept is an id, a type, a size, a page count and an expiry — nothing that would make this a library.
Every route that consumes a document now accepts both. The old form did not move, and no existing integration has to change a line.

head: Form
Where it comes from
Lifetime
rows: Kept until the deployment purges it.
An upload, or the output of a tool asked for as "output": "asset".
Two hours by default, then purged. DELETE /api/files/<id> is immediate.

blocks.text: Three ways to get the result out

head: What you send
What you get
When to use it
rows: The file must stay reachable by URL.
Another tool comes next. This is the one that makes a chain cheap.

blocks.html: A scanned contract arrives, has to be read, compressed, and handed back. Four calls, and the file never comes back down to the caller until the last one.

blocks.code:
# 1. Upload
SRC=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/files" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -F 'file=@scan.pdf' | jq -r '.files[0].id')

# 2. OCR — the result stays inside the service
OCRED=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/ocr" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"pdf\": \"asset://$SRC\", \"languages\": [\"fra\"], \"output\": \"asset\"}" \
  | jq -r '.asset.id')

# 3. Compress, and read the verdict rather than hoping
RESULT=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/compress" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"pdf\": \"asset://$OCRED\", \"level\": \"ebook\", \"output\": \"asset\"}")
echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.verdict.summary'   # 4.2 MB -> 780 KB, text intact
FINAL=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.asset.id')

# 4. Fetch the bytes, with the right content type
curl -s "$BASE/api/files/$FINAL" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" --output ready.pdf

blocks.html: GET /api/files/<id> serves the file with the content type of what it holds, while /download/… serves everything as application/pdf. That is why a tool that produces an image or a .docx tells you to ask for an asset.

blocks.text: When the work outlives the request

blocks.html: OCR on two hundred pages, a LibreOffice conversion or a Ghostscript pass on a heavy file do not fit inside a synchronous deadline. POST /api/jobs takes the endpoint name and the body it would have received, answers 202 with a poll URL, and forces the result to an asset — a job has no socket to stream a file down.

blocks.code:
JOB=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/jobs" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"endpoint": "ocr", "body": {"pdf": "asset://as_9f2c…", "languages": ["fra"]}}' \
  | jq -r '.job_id')

curl -s "$BASE/api/jobs/$JOB" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" | jq '{status, result: .result.asset.id}'
# {"status":"running","result":null} … then {"status":"done","result":"as_77aa…"}

blocks.html: The poll URL is the source of truth. A callback_url, when one is given, is a courtesy: sent once, signed with X-Signature, never retried. A webhook that must arrive exactly once is a message queue, and this service is not one.

blocks.text: What is kept, and for how long

head: Rule
Default
rows: 2 hours, then purged — configurable per deployment.

blocks.html: An expired asset answers 404, not a stale file. A chain that sits idle between two steps for longer than the retention will fail on the second one — which is the correct behaviour, and worth knowing before a nightly batch discovers it.

blocks.label: Upload a file from the console

guides.title: Preview, merge, watermark, protect
guides.lede: Four endpoints that operate on PDFs the service has already saved. They chain: the output of one is the input of the next.
guides.meta_description: Four endpoints that operate on PDFs the service has already saved. They chain: the output of one is the input of the next.

blocks.html: POST /api/preview takes the same body as a render (markdown, html, or template + data) and answers with images instead of a PDF. A body with no new field returns the PNG of page 1 — historical behaviour, unchanged.

head: Field
Default
Description
rows: png (raw image), images (JSON, one PNG per page), sheet (one contact-sheet image).

blocks.html: Without an explicit layout, one page returns a raw PNG and several return the images JSON — so an existing caller keeps getting exactly what it got. images reports truncated: true when the page cap cut the answer short; sheet cannot, since it is just an image.
POST /api/merge concatenates two or more previously saved PDFs, in the order given.
POST /api/watermark overlays a diagonal text watermark on every page of a saved PDF.

opacity defaults to 0.06 (0–1) and angle to -45 (−360 to 360). The default is deliberately faint: a watermark that fights the text makes the document unreadable, and an unreadable draft gets re-exported without the watermark.

Two watermarks, two purposes. options.watermark is drawn at render time, in CSS, under the text — it belongs to the document. /api/watermark stamps an existing PDF, including one the service did not produce.
POST /api/protect applies AES-256 password protection to a saved PDF. Do this last: an encrypted PDF cannot be merged, watermarked, previewed or diffed afterwards.

guides.title: The document contract
guides.lede: State what the document must satisfy instead of asking for a render. The service renders, audits, corrects, and answers with the log of what it had to do.
guides.meta_description: State what the document must satisfy instead of asking for a render. The service renders, audits, corrects, and answers with the log of what it had to do.

blocks.html: Every other endpoint answers here is your PDF, hope it is fine. POST /api/compose takes constraints: at most four pages, no table cut in half, a layout score of at least 90. It renders, audits with the Layout Doctor, applies corrective rules, re-renders, and stops when the contract holds or the passes run out — then hands back the file and what it had to do to get there.
Entirely deterministic: no model, no outbound call, and the same input produces the same document. That is what makes the render cache, the pixel diff and the attestation possible at all.
The body is a render body — markdown, or html, or template + data, plus the usual css and options — with one field more.

head: Field
Values
What it forbids
rows: A document that does not fit the envelope it was written for.
A table broken across two pages.
A heading stranded at the foot of a page.
A page produced by pagination and holding nothing.
Content reaching past the print area.
Anything the Layout Doctor grades below that mark.

blocks.html: Every field is optional, and a request with no constraint at all is simply a render with a report. max_passes defaults to 3 and is capped at 5: each pass is a full render, so a contract that needs more than a handful is a document problem rather than a layout problem, and saying so quickly is more useful than burning the whole time budget to fail anyway.
Send client_id + pdf_name (or "output": "asset") and you get the report; send neither and you get the PDF itself, as everywhere else.

verdict is met or unmet. passes is the honest part: it says what each attempt scored and which corrective rules it introduced, so a document that needed three passes today tells you where it is fragile before it needs four tomorrow.

A contract that could not be met still returns the best document produced, with verdict: "unmet" and unmet naming what is still broken. Refusing to hand it over would leave you with a report and nothing to look at. Check verdict — an HTTP 200 does not mean the contract held.

blocks.text: Sealing the result in the same call

blocks.html: Add "attest": true and the answer carries an attestation: the signed record of what was rendered, which POST /api/verify checks later. One call produces the document, its verdict and its proof.

guides.title: Proving a document came from us
guides.lede: A signed, self-contained record that says this file was issued here and has not been edited since. Two endpoints, no database, no lookup.
guides.meta_description: A signed, self-contained record that says this file was issued here and has not been edited since. Two endpoints, no database, no lookup.

blocks.html: A PDF says nothing about where it came from. An attestation does: hash of the file, page count, size, engine, theme, PDF variant, operations applied and the moment it was issued — serialised, signed with this deployment's key, and folded into a single line you can put in a header, a database column or an e-mail.

The record is self-contained on purpose: verifying it needs the file and that one line, never a lookup in a store we would then have to keep, back up and eventually leak. claims is the same record, readable, so you can show it without decoding anything.
The document is uploaded like any other — POST /api/files then asset:// — so a partner who received a PDF by mail can check it without ever having had an account here.

head: Verdict
What happened
What to do
rows: The signature matches and the file still hashes to what was sealed.
Nothing. This is the file that was issued.
The record is genuine, and the document no longer hashes to it.
The file was edited after issue. Ask for the original.
The signature does not belong to this deployment's key.
The record was tampered with — or it was issued by another service.
Not in the v1.<payload>.<signature> form, or a version this build does not read.
Copy-paste accident, most of the time. Check the whole line travelled.

blocks.html: altered and forged are deliberately told apart. They are different incidents — an edited document, or a fabricated record — and a single invalid would hide which one you are dealing with.

blocks.text: What it proves, and what it does not

blocks.html: An attestation proves origin and integrity against one deployment's key. It is not a qualified electronic signature: it carries no identity, no certificate and no legal timestamp. When a document has to be signed in the legal sense, that is a different apparatus, and this one does not pretend to replace it.

The signing key is the deployment's. Set ATTESTATION_SECRET (16 characters at least) and attestations survive a restart and can be checked by any instance sharing it; leave it unset and the service draws a key at startup, says so in its logs, and every attestation stops verifying at the next restart. That is the honest failure: an attestation nobody can check is better than one anybody can forge.
The natural pairing is with the contract: POST /api/compose with "attest": true renders the document, grades it, and seals it in one call — the file, its verdict and its proof, produced together.

guides.title: Five complete recipes
guides.lede: Whole workflows, copy-pasteable, each combining several features the way a real integration does.
guides.meta_description: Whole workflows, copy-pasteable, each combining several features the way a real integration does.

blocks.html: Cover page, brand kit, numbering, table of contents, draft watermark, then AES-256. Four calls, each feeding the next.

One source, two PDFs. The free edition keeps the CENSOR tags; the paid edition has them stripped before the call. Same theme, same pagination, same figures — which is what makes the hole read as a paywall rather than as a broken document.

blocks.code:
# Free edition — the source ships with its tags
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/convert" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @study.json \
  --output study-free.pdf

# Paid edition — same JSON, tags removed from the `markdown` field first
jq '.markdown |= gsub("\\{\\{CENSOR:[^}]*\\}\\}"; "")' study.json \
  | curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/convert" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- --output study-full.pdf

blocks.html: One Tera template, one JSON context per invoice, no theme and no autolayout — this is the path built for volume. The template is stored on your side and sent with each call, so a change of wording is a deploy of your service, not of ours.

Identical inputs hit the content-addressed render cache and come back with cached: true without re-rendering. Two invoices differ, so they will not — but a re-run of the same batch after a failure costs almost nothing.
Render the same document on both branches, compare, fail the build if anything moved. The threshold stays at 0 so a renamed heading is caught.

blocks.code:
render() {  # $1 = name — renders the reference document and saves it
  curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/convert" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "$(jq -n --rawfile md fixtures/reference.md --arg n "$1" \
         '{markdown: $md, options: {theme: "report@1"}, client_id: "ci", pdf_name: $n}')" \
    | jq -r .download_url
}

BEFORE=$(git stash && render main && git stash pop)
AFTER=$(render branch)

VERDICT=$(curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/diff" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"before\": \"$BEFORE\", \"after\": \"$AFTER\", \"threshold\": 0}" | jq -r .verdict)

[ "$VERDICT" = identical ] || { echo "rendering changed"; exit 1; }

blocks.html: A supplier contract has to go to a partner, minus the personal data and the bank details. Redact first, then compare the result against the source: the pages the diff reports as changed must be exactly the pages the redaction says it painted. Two independent answers agreeing is what makes it a check rather than a hope.

blocks.code:
# 1. Redact — JSON form, because we want the counts back
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/redact" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
    "pdf": "/download/legal/supplier-contract.pdf",
    "entities": ["email", "iban", "phone"],
    "patterns": ["Jean Dupont"],
    "client_id": "legal", "pdf_name": "supplier-contract-public"
  }'
# {"redactions":[{"page":1,"count":4},{"page":3,"count":2}],"mode":"flatten",…}
#
# An empty `redactions` array here means nothing was FOUND — check the source
# has a text layer before concluding it had nothing to hide.

# 2. Compare source and result: pages 1 and 3 must be the ones that moved
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/diff" -H "X-API-Key: $MDTOPDF_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
    "before": "/download/legal/supplier-contract.pdf",
    "after":  "/download/legal/supplier-contract-public.pdf",
    "threshold": 0
  }' | jq '.per_page'

blocks.html: The redacted file is rebuilt from pixels, so every page differs from its source at the byte level. The diff still tells you what you need: per_page ranks the pages by how much visibly changed, and a page that only lost a text layer barely moves while a page that gained a black rectangle does.

guides.title: Limits, caching and safety
guides.lede: What the service refuses, what it remembers, and what it does when it is busy. Reading this before going to production is cheaper than reading it after.
guides.meta_description: What the service refuses, what it remembers, and what it does when it is busy. Reading this before going to production is cheaper than reading it after.

blocks.html: Renders run in a bounded pool. Past the pool, requests queue; past the queue timeout, you get a 429 with a Retry-After header telling you when a retry has a chance. A whole job — render, preview, redaction or diff, every process and every corrective pass together — is bounded by a single wall-clock deadline, so a request can never outlive the proxy in front of it.

blocks.html: Rendering is content-addressed: the key hashes the expanded source, your CSS, the engine, the resolved options, the header and footer, and the theme name@version. Identical inputs come back instantly with cached: true. Two consequences are worth knowing before you go looking for a purge endpoint — there is none.

Changing anything that reaches the key invalidates nothing and evicts nothing; it simply produces a different key, and both entries coexist until TTL or LRU drops them. And changing a published theme.css in place does not change the key at all — which is why theme versions exist.

WeasyPrint dereferences every URL a document points at, so two layers stand in the way. The request is rejected with a 400 naming the offending URL when the document or your CSS references file://, a private address, a cloud metadata endpoint, or a host outside the allowlist. At render time the fetcher re-checks every URL, re-resolving DNS and pinning the validated IP — a remote resource that is refused is simply absent from the PDF rather than an error.
This is why weasyprint is the default and the only engine available without a token. wkhtmltopdf and pdflatex only get the first layer — the guarded fetcher has no equivalent there.

Every response carries an X-Request-Id. Send your own on the way in — printable ASCII, 128 characters at most — and it is echoed back and attached to every log event the request produces, including the render event with its duration, engine and cache status. That identifier is what turns "a PDF came out wrong yesterday" into a line in a log.

POST / takes FormData and is not covered by the API key — it never was, by design, so existing integrations keep working. Being open is what shapes what it offers: it renders with weasyprint only, block expansion is off (a ```mermaid fence stays a code listing, so an anonymous body of them cannot turn one request into thousands of outbound calls), and a blocked URL is reported rather than fatal. /api/* behaves the other way round on all three counts.
